**Sprint 3: Nov 3 to Nov 19, 100 points (12% of course).**
- **Deadlines:** D7 check-in plus at least one code PR you authored (open and ready, or merged) due **Nov 12, 11:59 PM**. Everything else, including the D10 survey, due **Nov 19, 11:59 PM**. No late policy stated (syllabus: 2-hour grace, then 10% per day).
- **Zero rule:** no merged PR (D4), no report (D8) or no release (D9) gives the team 0 for the sprint.
- **Points:** D1 backlog 10 (team), D2 spec 20, D3 design 5, D4 PRs 20 (averaged, scaled to 20), D5 AI logs 5, D6 mutation 15, D7 check-in 5, D8 report 10 (team), D9 release 2 (team), D10 reflection survey 8 (link via Blackboard/Zulip near sprint end).
- **Graded strictly:** code PR open by the check-in; merge only after a teammate approves the **latest commit**; spec review comment on the issue saying what was checked (each AC clear and testable, cases and whether ACs cover them, scope fit), "Looks good!" alone is not acceptable; `Closes #N` plus issue and PR on the `Sprint 3` milestone; real AI logs; report renders (no escaped `\|` or `\[`).
- **D1 load:** CSCI 435 = at least 2 medium issues (or equivalent points); one assignee per issue; each issue states small/medium scope with 1-2 sentences why (TA may reclassify). Sprint 2 carryovers go in first or are dropped with a reason on the issue. Optional: one issue may be a hardening issue. The instructor/TA posts a Sprints 3-4 team feature as an issue; its sub-issues (owner, spec, scope, linked, on milestone) count toward load. It is #20 (posted by 2026-11-07; sub-issues #143-145, all ab-wm's).
- **Hardening evidence:** bug fix = failing-then-passing test; flaky = root cause plus 20 unit / 10 E2E runs before and after; CI check = run links before and after; baseline failures = counts before and after with causes. Reformatting, regenerating snapshots or silencing a check counts as small at most.
- **D2/D3:** spec reviewed before coding; each design decision names at least two concrete alternatives and why one won (issue body, issue comment or PR all count).
- **D4 PRs:** `## Test Evidence` table `Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value`, one row per AC; levels unit/integration/E2E/manual; sources AC, issue discussion, docs, upstream behavior, other; "the current output of your own code is not a valid source". Plus `**Not tested automatically, and why:**` and `**AI-written tests:**` ("None." if none). `## Tech Debt` with `**Introduced:**` and `**Encountered:**` ("None." valid). Rubric: ACs 6, tests and Test Evidence 6, description/Tech Debt/issue link 3, CI or documented manual checks 3, rubric review and approval on latest commit 2. Reviewers respond within 24 hours.
- **D6 mutation testing:** one issue whose PR changes source and tests; a tool is required (StrykerJS + Vitest runner for frontend, Gremlins or go-mutesting for Go; the team chose go-mutesting, see `.claude-students/docs/mutation-testing.md`). Run only on the PR's changed files. Analyse every survivor (at least 10 if more), add a test that kills a gap survivor and re-run. Files: `docs/sprint3/mutation/<issue#>-<user>.md` and `reports/<issue#>-<user>-{before,after}.json` (`.txt` for go-mutesting). Rubric: run and reports 4, survivors 4, killing test 4, answers 3. Blockers go to the TA early.
- **D7 check-in:** `docs/sprint3/checkin/<user>.md`, about 100 words each on: done and remaining; one thing learned about testing; one risk and the plan. On time with a PR linked = 5; late, thin or no PR = 3; missing = 0.
- **D8 report:** Sprint 1 sections plus Suite health (baseline at tag `v1.27.3-csci435-s2` and at sprint end, failures grouped by cause with one issue each, no new failures, skipped tests need an issue and a code comment), links to D6 files, hardening issues, carryovers.
- **D9:** tag `v1.27.3-csci435-s3` after the last merge, plus a GitHub release summarising features, fixes and hardening.
- **Extra credit:** up to 3 per upstream PR accepted or under active review, up to 2 per upstream bug confirmed by Sprint 4 grading.

**AI logs (all sprints):** `ai-logs/sprint<N>/<github-username>/YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<slug>.md` (tool id e.g. `claude-code`), attachments in a same-named folder, `.md`/`.txt`/`.json` only. Full prompts and output; summaries, paraphrases, share links or output without prompts don't count. One AI Assistance comment per contributor per issue worked, linking the log file itself, or "No AI used." Unproductive sessions get logged too.

**Carried from Sprints 1-2:** no self-approval or self-merge; each student reviews at least one PR per sprint; branch deleted after merge.

**Reading the rules:** the course site wins over `.claude-students/COURSE-WORKFLOW.md`. Where the repo doc is stricter (D3 in the issue body only, the exact `Spec reviewed` opener), present it as team convention, not a grading risk. A missing design section at spec review is a reminder, never a blocker.

**Why:** I twice over-read the design rule from the repo doc instead of the site (#55 in Sprint 1; #56/#58/#59 spec reviews on 2026-10-18). PR #94's rewrite of the course rules also missed site rules until CodeRabbit flagged them.
**How to apply:** Quote the site before flagging a deliverable problem. When a new sprint starts, re-fetch and rewrite this file. See [[sprint-history]], [[ai-log-tooling]].

```text
# Course workflow — issues, PRs, reviews, sprint deliverables

Course rules, not upstream Gitea ones. Source: the course site <https://csci-435-se.github.io/>
(Sprints pages and Glossary) and `docs/sprint0/standards.md`. Everyone on the team, and every AI
session, uses the formats below so all issues and PRs look the same. The GitHub templates in
`.github/` carry the same formats; if they ever disagree with this page, fix the template.

AI disclosure has its own page: `AI-ASSISTANCE.md`.

## Current sprint: Sprint 3

- **Dates:** Nov 3 – Nov 19, 2026. Everything pushed and merged by **Nov 19, 11:59 PM**, except
  the D7 check-in, due **Nov 12, 11:59 PM** together with at least one code PR of your own, open
  and ready for review or merged.
- **Focus:** testing, meaning how well the tests check what the code is supposed to do.
- **Points:** 100.
- **Zero rule:** no merged PR (D4), no sprint report (D8) or no release (D9) means **0 for the
  whole sprint**.
- **Carries forward:** anything the Sprint 3 page doesn't change comes from the Sprint 2 and
  Sprint 1 pages, and every Sprint 0 standard still applies.
- **Start early:** record the test baseline at the Sprint 2 tag (see D8), and get the mutation tool
  running on any existing file in your area (see D6) before your PRs are ready.

| # | Deliverable | Points | Who | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | Sprint backlog: a `Sprint 3` milestone with every selected issue on it, each with a justified scope | 10 | Team | GitHub milestone |
| D2 | Requirements spec for each issue (formats below), spec-reviewed on the issue before coding | 20 | Individual | Issue body |
| D3 | At least one non-trivial design decision per issue, with **at least two alternatives** | 5 | Individual | Issue body |
| D4 | Code changes and PRs, each with `## Test Evidence` and `## Tech Debt` sections | 20 | Individual | PRs |
| D5 | AI logs | 5 | Individual | `ai-logs/sprint3/<github-username>/` |
| D6 | Mutation testing on one issue's PR (CSCI 535: two) | 15 | Individual | `docs/sprint3/mutation/` |
| D7 | Mid-sprint check-in, linking a code PR | 5 | Individual | `docs/sprint3/checkin/<github-username>.md` |
| D8 | Sprint report, with a Suite health section | 10 | Team | `docs/sprint3/report.md` |
| D9 | Release: tag `v1.27.3-csci435-s3` plus a GitHub release | 2 | Team | Tags / Releases |
| D10 | Reflection survey | 8 | Individual | Blackboard/Zulip link |

### Graded strictly this sprint

The Sprint 3 page lists these as the rules that cost the most points. Details are in the sections
named.

1. No merge without a teammate's approval on the PR's **latest commit** (Reviews, below).
2. A spec review comment on the issue that says what was checked (Spec review, under the issue
   formats).
3. Every code PR has `Closes #<N>`, and both the issue and the PR are on the `Sprint 3` milestone.
4. Real AI logs, linked from the issue (D5).
5. A Test Evidence table in every PR, with expected values not copied from the code's output
   (Pull request format).
6. Mutation testing with a tool, with before and after reports committed (Mutation testing (D6)).
7. The team introduces no new test failures. A skipped test or a disabled CI check needs a linked
   issue and a reason in a code comment (D8).
8. A sprint report that renders on GitHub and uses the Sprint 3 sections (D8).

### Deliverable notes

- **D1 load:** each CSCI 435 student owns at least 2 medium issues; each CSCI 535 student owns at
  least 2 medium and 1 small. Either load can be met with equivalent story points instead. Every
  issue has exactly **one** assignee. Unfinished Sprint 2 issues go into the backlog before new
  work. To drop one, write the reason on that issue. If the backlog is too thin to meet the load,
  find areas that still need work (features, improvements, test gaps, bugs) and write new issues
  for them the usual way.
- **D1 scope:** every issue states its scope (small or medium) and one or two sentences on why:
  which components it touches and how much change is expected. The instructor or TA may reclassify
  an issue whose scope is clearly overstated.
- **D1 hardening issues (optional):** one of your issues may be a hardening issue. See "Hardening
  issues" below.
- **D1 team feature:** the instructor or TA posts a larger feature for Sprints 3–4 as an issue and
  tells the team. Split it into sub-issues, each with one owner, its own spec (D2) and scope, linked
  to the feature issue and added to the `Sprint 3` milestone. Sub-issues count toward the load.
- **D2:** specs are written and spec-reviewed before coding starts. Features use the user story
  format; hardening issues use the bug report format when they fix a defect, otherwise the
  hardening task format.
- **D3:** each decision names at least two concrete alternatives and why one won; this is graded
  strictly. The site also accepts the decision in an issue comment or the PR description; the team
  keeps it in the issue body. Decisions that span issues go in `docs/sprint3/design.md`.
- **D4:** every PR description has the Test Evidence and Tech Debt sections (see "Pull request
  format"). Per-PR scores are combined across your PRs and scaled to 20.
- **D5:** conventions are in `ai-logs/README.md`. Logs hold the full prompts and output. Graded
  strictly this sprint: a session summary, paraphrased prompts, a share link, or tool output without
  the prompts that produced it is not a log. The link must open the log file itself, not a folder
  or another issue. The folder must exist even if no AI was used; in that case, post a comment
  saying so. The site accepts the link from the issue or the PR; the team keeps it in **issue
  comments only** (`AI-ASSISTANCE.md`).
- **D6:** see "Mutation testing (D6)" below.
- **D7:** about 100 words on each of: what you have implemented so far and what remains; one thing
  you learned about testing in the project; one risk to finishing by Nov 19 and what you will do
  about it. Link at least one **code PR you authored**, open and ready for review or merged, by Nov
  12. On time, substantive and with a PR linked scores 5; late, thin or no PR 3; missing 0.
- **D8:** graded on completeness, specificity, quality of evidence and the Suite health section;
  sections are in "Sprint report (D8) sections" below.
- **D9:** keep the base version (`v1.27.3-csci435-s2` → `v1.27.3-csci435-s3`). Tag **after the
  last Sprint 3 merge**, so the release matches the final `main`, and push the tag to origin. The
  release description summarizes the sprint's features, fixes and hardening work, not just the tag
  name.
- **Reviews:** nobody approves or merges their own PR. Request the review on GitHub and tell the
  reviewer on Zulip; reviewers respond (approve or request changes) within 24 hours, with
  substantive comments and the rubric, not a bare approval. A PR is merged only after a teammate
  approves its **latest commit**: any push after the approval, including merging `main` in, needs
  a new approval. Once approved, the author merges. Each student reviews at least one PR per
  sprint, and every teammate at least once per semester.
- **Extra credit:** up to 3 points per PR submitted to upstream Gitea that is accepted or under
  active review, and up to 2 points per bug report filed upstream that comes from your own testing
  and is confirmed by the maintainers by the time Sprint 4 is graded. Both at the instructor's
  discretion.

## Branches and commits

- Branches: `feat/issue-<N>-short-description`, `fix/issue-<N>-short-description` or
  `chore/short-description` (`STUDENTS.md`). One issue per branch.
- Commit messages follow Conventional Commits and end with the issue number:
  `feat(repo): show empty state on releases page (#17)`. Add an
  `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer when AI helped; never `Co-Authored-By` or
  `Signed-off-by` (`AGENTS.md`). A human approves every commit before it is made.

### Before each implementation: sync with main

Every new branch starts from an up-to-date `main`. AI sessions run this before writing any code:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch -c feat/issue-<N>-short-description
```

To pick up new work on `main` for a branch that already exists, **merge, don't rebase**. Rebasing
or squashing after review has started is not allowed (`docs/sprint0/standards.md`):

```bash
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
```

Do this before opening the PR and again if `main` moves while it is in review. A merge pushed after
approval needs a new approval (see Reviews). Never merge another feature branch into yours.

### After merge: clean up

A PR is merged with a merge commit once its latest commit is approved, every review comment is
addressed and CI passes. Then:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git branch -d feat/issue-<N>-short-description               # local branch
git push origin --delete feat/issue-<N>-short-description    # or GitHub's "Delete branch" button
git fetch --prune                                            # drop stale remote-tracking refs
```

Also check that the issue closed (via `Closes #N`), that the issue and PR are on the sprint
milestone, and that the issue has its AI Assistance comment. Then run `specstory sync` and file the
session's log (see `ai-logs/README.md`).

## Issue format: feature (user story)

Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user-story.yaml`. The user story must meet INVEST: Independent,
Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

```markdown
## User Story
As a <role>, I want <capability> so that <benefit>.

## User Scenario
<A short concrete walk-through: who, where in the UI, what they do, what they see.>

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given <state>, when <action>, then <observable result>.
- [ ] AC2: ...
- [ ] AC3: ...            (at least 3; each has a clear pass/fail result)

## Out of Scope
- <What this issue deliberately does not do.>

## Open Questions
- <Unresolved questions, or "None".>

## Design Decision
**Decision:** <what was chosen>
**Alternatives Considered:** <at least two concrete options, and why each lost>
**Rationale:** <why this one>
**Consequences:** <trade-offs, follow-up work, what it makes harder>

## Scope
small | medium | large, and matching `scope:` label
<One or two sentences on why: the components it touches and how much change you expect.>
```

## Issue format: bug report

Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug-report.yaml`. Also used by hardening issues that fix a
defect.

```markdown
## Observed Behavior
## Expected Behavior
## Steps to Reproduce
1. ...
## Additional Information
<Version or commit, browser/OS, logs, screenshots.>
## Design Decision
<Same four fields as above: Decision, Alternatives Considered, Rationale, Consequences.>
### User Story

As a reviewer, I want to suggest an exact code change in a review comment, and as the PR author, I want to apply it with one click, so that small fixes don't need to be explained and retyped.

### User Scenario

A reviewer selects a few lines in a pull request diff and writes the code she would like to see instead. The PR author sees her suggestion as a diff in the conversation, clicks to apply it, and Gitea adds a commit with that change to the PR branch.

### Acceptance Criteria

The criteria below are a starting point and are incomplete. The open questions must be answered before implementation.

- [ ] AC1: Given selected lines in a PR diff, when a reviewer adds a suggestion, then the comment shows the suggested change as a diff.
- [ ] AC2: Given a suggestion, when the PR author applies it, then a commit with the change is added to the PR branch.
- [ ] AC3: Given a user who can't push to the PR branch, when they try to apply a suggestion, then nothing is committed and they see why.
- [ ] More criteria needed, based on the open questions below.

Acceptance criteria should also cover invalid input, failures, conflicts, and permissions, not only the main path.

### Out of Scope

- Suggestions on commits outside a pull request
- Suggestions that create, rename, or delete files

### Open Questions

- What happens if the code changed after the suggestion was made?
- Who besides the PR author may apply a suggestion? What about pull requests from forks?
- What if the PR is closed or merged, or its branch was deleted?
- Can several suggestions be applied at once? What if they touch the same lines?
- Who appears as the author of the commit?
- What happens if two people apply suggestions at the same time?

## Issue format: hardening task

No GitHub template; write it in a blank issue. Used by hardening issues that don't fix a defect,
such as a flaky test or a broken CI check (Sprint 3, D2).

```markdown
## Problem
<What is unreliable now, and how you know: failing test names, run counts, CI run links.>
## Goal
<What "fixed" means.>
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: ...
## Evidence of Fix
<Which evidence from the table below the fix will show.>
## Design Decision
<Same four fields as above.>
## Scope
<Same as above: size, label and one or two sentences on why.>
```

### Hardening issues

Work that makes the existing system more reliable rather than adding a feature. Good sources: the
D8 baseline run (failing or flaky tests, broken CI checks on `main`); the "Introduced" and
"Encountered" Tech Debt fields of Sprint 1 and Sprint 2 PRs; bugs found in reviews or after
merging; and the upstream issue tracker for the parts of Gitea the team works on. It is scoped like
any other issue and must include evidence that the problem is fixed:

| Kind | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Bug fix | A test that fails before the fix and passes after |
| Flaky test | The root cause, and repeated runs before and after the fix (e.g. 20 for a unit test, 10 for E2E) |
| Broken or missing CI check | Links to CI runs before and after the fix |
| Failing tests in the baseline | Pass/fail counts before and after, and the cause of each group of failures |

The site doesn't say where the evidence goes: plan it in the issue (Evidence of Fix, or Additional
Information for a bug), then post the results on the issue and in the PR's Test Evidence once the
fix is in. Regenerating snapshots, reformatting code, or silencing a check without fixing its cause
counts as small at most.

### Design Decision and spec review

- **Design Decision (D3):** fill it in once you've picked an approach, before opening the PR. Put
  a second decision under another `### Decision 2` heading. If a PR changes the decision, update
  the issue body.
- **Spec review (D2):** before coding starts, a teammate posts a review comment **on the issue**.
  Start it with `Spec reviewed` so it is easy to find. The layout is the reviewer's choice, but the
  comment must say what was checked:
  1. each acceptance criterion: clear and testable, naming any that aren't;
  2. the cases considered (e.g. empty input, errors, permissions) and whether the ACs cover them;
  3. whether the scope fits the stated size;

  and end with an approval, or the problems for the author to fix in the spec. `Looks good!` with
  nothing about what was checked does not count. An optional layout:

  ```markdown
  Spec reviewed — @reviewer-username

  **Acceptance criteria:** <clear and testable? which aren't, and why>
  **Cases considered:** <which cases, and whether the ACs cover them>
  **Scope:** <does it fit the stated size?>
  **Verdict:** Approved | Changes needed: <list>
  ```

## Pull request format

Template: `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Title uses Conventional Commits, e.g.
`fix(issues): keep label filter after search`. Description sections:

1. `Closes #<N>`, which links the issue and closes it on merge. Every code PR links its issue, and
   the PR goes on the `Sprint 3` milestone too.
2. **What changed:** the change in your own words.
3. **Why:** the problem, and which acceptance criteria (AC1…) it satisfies.
4. **Test Evidence:** required from Sprint 3. It replaces the old "How it was tested" section.
   Every behaviour change still needs a new or updated test.

   ```markdown
   ## Test Evidence

   | Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | AC1: ... | ... | ... | ... |

   **Not tested automatically, and why:** [...]

   **AI-written tests:** [Which tests were written or modified by AI, and how you checked that their expected values are correct. If none, write "None."]
   ```

   - **One row per acceptance criterion** from the issue; for a bug report, the Expected Behavior.
     A PR that changes no product behaviour (e.g. a CI change) writes `N/A` and why.
   - **Test(s):** the test name, plus the file if not obvious. For a manual check, write `Manual:`
     followed by the steps and what you saw. An AC tested both ways lists both in the same row.
   - **Level:** `unit`, `integration`, `E2E` or `manual`.
   - **Source of expected value:** `AC`, `issue discussion`, `docs`, `upstream behavior`, or
     `other` (explain). **Never the current output of your own code:** a test whose expected value
     was copied from what the code returns cannot detect that the code is wrong.
   - **Not tested automatically, and why:** only for ACs checked manually only.
   - AI may draft this section; the author checks that it is accurate.

5. **CI / manual verification:** CI status. If CI doesn't run your tests, the commands you ran and
   a summary of the results (passed, failed, skipped).
6. **Design:** one line pointing at the Design Decision in the issue, or a note on how it changed.
7. **Tech Debt:** required from Sprint 2. Both fields are required, and `None.` is a valid answer:

   ```markdown
   ## Tech Debt

   **Introduced:** <shortcuts, workarounds or design compromises this PR makes, and why>

   **Encountered:** <tech debt that was already there and that you ran into, and how you handled it>
   ```

8. **AI assistance:** format in `AI-ASSISTANCE.md` §2, with **no log link**.

Per-PR grading (20 points): correctness against the acceptance criteria 6; tests written or updated
appropriately, with the Test Evidence section complete, every AC covered and expected values

// CanComment returns whether a line can get commented
func (d *DiffLine) CanComment() bool {
	return len(d.Comments) == 0 && d.Type != DiffLineSection
}

// GetCommentSide returns the comment side of the first comment, if not set returns empty string
func (d *DiffLine) GetCommentSide() string {
	if len(d.Comments) == 0 {
		return ""
	}
	return d.Comments[0].DiffSide()
}

// GetLineTypeMarker returns the line type marker
func (d *DiffLine) GetLineTypeMarker() string {
	if strings.IndexByte(" +-", d.Content[0]) > -1 {
		return d.Content[0:1]
	}
	return ""
}

`````markdown
### User Story

Labels: `enhancement`, `scope: small` · Type: Feature · Part of #151

As a reviewer, I want a button that fills in a suggestion block with the current line so that I
only edit the code instead of copying it and remembering the syntax.

### User Scenario

Ana opens the Files tab of an open PR and clicks the `+` next to new-side line 18. The code
comment form that opens has a "Suggest change" button in its toolbar. She clicks it and the
textarea gets a ```` ```suggestion ```` block holding line 18's current text, with the cursor at the
end of that line inside the block. She edits the line and clicks "Add single comment". The comment
is saved with the block as she typed it; showing it as a diff is S1's job.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC1: Given the code comment form opened on a new-side line (an added line, or an unchanged
  context line, including lines revealed by "expand"), in split or unified view, when the reviewer
  clicks "Suggest change", then the textarea contains a block made of a fence line
  ```` ```suggestion ````, the line's exact text (leading tabs and spaces kept, no `+` or space
  diff marker, no highlighting markup), and a closing fence.
- [ ] AC2: Given the textarea already has text, when the reviewer clicks "Suggest change", then the
  block is inserted at the cursor (replacing any selected text), starts on a line of its own and is
  followed by a newline, and the text before and after it is kept.
- [ ] AC3: Given the block was just inserted, then the textarea has focus and the cursor sits at
  the end of the line's text inside the block.
- [ ] AC4: Given the line's text contains a run of N backticks with N ≥ 3 (for example
  ```` ```js ````), when the block is inserted, then both fences use N+1 backticks, so the block
  is not closed early. With fewer than 3 backticks in a row, the fences stay at 3.
- [ ] AC5: Given an empty or whitespace-only line, when the block is inserted, then the block
  holds that line as is (an empty line or the same whitespace) between the fences.
- [ ] AC6: Given the form opened on an old-side line (a deleted line, or the left column of a
  changed line in split view), when the form is shown, then the "Suggest change" button is not
  shown. If the customer's answer to question 5 on #151 allows old-side suggestions, this AC is
  updated before coding starts.
- [ ] AC7: Given any markdown editor other than the code comment form (issue or PR conversation
  comment, review summary, editing an existing comment, a reply in an existing conversation), when
  it is shown, then it has no "Suggest change" button.
- [ ] AC8: Given a visitor who is not signed in, or a repository that is archived, when the Files
  tab is shown, then there is no code comment form and so no button (behaviour unchanged,
  regression test).
- [ ] AC9: Given a merged or closed PR, when the reviewer opens the code comment form, then the
  button is shown and works as in AC1 (Gitea still allows code comments there). If the customer
  answers that suggestions on closed PRs should be blocked, this AC is updated before coding.
- [ ] AC10: The button is a keyboard-focusable `<button>` with an accessible name and tooltip
  from a new locale key `repo.diff.comment.suggest_change` (English "Suggest change", added to
  `locale_en-US.json` only).
- [ ] AC11: Given a comment with a suggestion block, when it is submitted, then the stored comment
  content is exactly the textarea text (no server-side change to comment content).

### Out of Scope

- Selecting several lines (S5).
- Rendering the block as a diff (S1) and applying it (S3).
- The button in reply forms of an existing conversation. A line that already has a conversation
  has no `+`, so suggestions there wait for a later issue.
- The legacy EasyMDE editor: switching to it hides the button, and switching back shows it again.
- Server-side checks on suggestion blocks. The server stores them as plain markdown.

### Open Questions

- Customer question 5 on #151: are suggestions on the old (deleted) side allowed? AC6 assumes no.
- New question for the customer: should a reviewer be able to write a suggestion on a merged or
  closed PR, where it can never be applied? AC9 assumes yes, since the form is already there.

### Design Decision

**Decision:** Read the line text from the diff row already in the DOM (the `.code-inner` cell of
the row the form belongs to, as `textContent`) and insert it with the existing
`replaceTextareaSelection` helper from `EditorMarkdown.ts`; no server call. The button is added to
the shared markdown toolbar only when the editor sits inside a code comment form for the right
side.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- *Fetch the raw line from the server.* Exact, but a round trip for text already on the page, and a
  new endpoint with its own permission checks.
- *Server-render the block into the form's initial value.* Forces a suggestion on every comment and
  the reviewer has to delete it for a plain comment.

**Rationale:** The diff row holds the exact text the reviewer is looking at, which is what the
suggestion is anchored to.

**Consequences:** Depends on the diff row markup; highlighted spans must be read as plain text
(`textContent`), and an e2e test guards it. If the markup changes upstream, the e2e test fails
instead of the button inserting the wrong text.

### Decision 2

**Decision:** Build the fences from backticks, one longer than the longest backtick run in the line
and never shorter than 3. The text-building function is pure and unit-tested in Vitest.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- *Always use 3 backticks.* Breaks on any line holding ```` ``` ````, such as markdown files or
  code that embeds fenced blocks.
- *Use a tilde fence (`~~~suggestion`).* Fails the same way on lines holding `~~~`, and S1's
  renderer would need to accept both fence styles.

**Rationale:** CommonMark closes a fence only on a run at least as long as the opening one, so a
longer opening fence always holds the line, whatever it contains.

**Consequences:** S1's parser must accept suggestion fences longer than 3 backticks.

### Scope

small

### Scope Justification

Frontend only: one toolbar button in the shared markdown editor template shown for code comment
forms, a small TypeScript module with a pure text builder (Vitest) and the click handler, one
locale key, and one Playwright e2e test. No Go, database, API or permission changes.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-11 19:46:24Z)**_

No, S2 doesn't depend on S1 or on any other sub-issue, and no other sub-issue lists it as a dependency.

**Why it stands alone:** S2 only inserts text into the comment box, and the server stores that text as ordinary markdown. You can build, test and merge it before S1. Until S1 lands, the suggestion block just shows up as a plain code block.

**What does tie it to S1 and S3 (#156)** is the block format: a ```` ```suggestion ```` fence holding the line's exact text, with longer fences when the line contains backticks. S1 renders that format and S3 applies it, so if any of the three changes the format, the other two have to change too.

**Dependencies between the other sub-issues:**

| Issue | Depends on |
| --- | --- |
| S1 #154 | none |
| S2 #155 | none |
| S3 #156 | S1 |
| S4 #157 | S3 |
| S5 #158 | S1, S3 |
| S6 #159 | S3, S4 |

S5 doesn't list S2, but multi-line suggestions will probably need to extend your button. Your Out of Scope section already hands multi-line selection to S5. The Sprint 3 demo doesn't strictly need S2 either, since a reviewer can type the block by hand.
